the pharmacokinetics of an antibiotic in serum are not necessarily a good indicator of its pharmacodynamics in phagocytes; and that the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic relationship is not the same for all antibiotics and all intracellular pathogens.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are still in the dark about the clinical relevance of these data.
the intracellular concentration of antibiotics in phagocytic cells is not a function of the serum concentration of the drug.
the intracellular activity of antibiotics is a complex function of their pharmacokinetics and their interaction with the host cell, and that the latter is still poorly understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the serum concentrations of antibiotics are not always good indicators of the concentrations that are achieved in the phagocytes, which may explain the clinical efficacy of some of the antibiotics in the treatment of intracellular infections.
the serum concentrations of antibiotics are not a good predictor of the antibiotic activity in patients.
the serum levels of antibiotics are not the only factor determining the efficacy of an antibiotic in the treatment of intracellular infections.
